messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 53
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Social Worker
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 52

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Enclosed Spaces: Enclosed or confined spaces, Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant, Thought Suppression: I try to push them out of my mind
  Threat: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
  Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Daniel was 53, a married social worker, and by the time he came for help he was describing a life that had become carefully narrowed around a single night he had never managed to leave behind. The assault had happened years earlier, when he was alone in a place that should have felt ordinary and contained. What remained most vivid for him was not a coherent story he could tell easily, but a set of fragments he could still feel in his body: the crushing terror of being trapped, the humiliating sense of being overpowered, and the immediate shame that followed when he tried to make sense of what had happened. Even now, when he tried to speak about it, Daniel would pause and search for language, saying he knew exactly what had happened but could not find the words that felt adequate to describe it. In sessions, his voice would tighten and he would fall back on short, factual statements, as though anything more detailed might expose him to the same mortification he felt then.

In the months after the assault, Daniel found himself trying to force the memory away whenever it rose up. He would push it out of his mind, only to have it return later in a flood of terror that felt indistinguishable from the original moment. At times, recalling it brought back the same raw panic he had felt during the assault, as if the event were not over but still unfolding somewhere just beyond the present. He also noticed that his mind kept returning to thoughts of revenge. He would ruminate about how he might get even with the assailant, not because he expected to act on it, but because the thoughts gave him a fleeting sense that he had not been made entirely helpless. He was ashamed of these thoughts too, and the shame seemed to accumulate alongside the memory itself.

Over time, Daniel began organizing his days around the sense that danger could appear without warning. He frequently looked behind him when he walked, scanning for anyone who might be following him. If he arrived somewhere and the route or layout was unfamiliar, he would avoid going in at all, telling himself he could not assess the danger quickly enough. At work, this meant turning down assignments that would have taken him into new neighborhoods or unfamiliar buildings. As a social worker, his job required him to move between offices, homes, and community sites, and he found himself planning routes obsessively or asking for details long before leaving the office. What had once been routine visits became tense calculations about entrances, exits, and who might be nearby. If a meeting ran longer than expected or a client was delayed, his mind jumped immediately to the thought that something bad was happening. He would stare at his phone, growing increasingly unsettled by each passing minute, certain that delay meant threat until proven otherwise.

His avoidance extended into enclosed spaces as well. Daniel came to dread elevators, small conference rooms, and any place that felt confined or hard to leave. In such spaces his body would tense, and he would count the seconds until he could get out. He began choosing stairs when he could and standing near doors in meetings, even when this made him look distracted or disengaged. At home, his wife noticed him circling his routines so that he would not have to enter places that felt boxed in, and she also noticed how little he wanted to talk about the assault. When she asked, he would shut down or change the subject, not because he did not trust her, but because the shame came so quickly that he felt almost physically unable to stay with the conversation.

By the time he sought treatment, Daniel’s world had become smaller and more exhausting. He was still working, but with increasing effort, and he felt embarrassed by how often he checked over his shoulder or hesitated at a doorway like someone much younger and less in control. What brought him in was the accumulation of these moments: the strain on his marriage, the narrowing of his work, and his growing fear that he would keep living as though the assault were happening all over again. He said he wanted to be able to name what happened without feeling overwhelmed, to sit in a room without automatically looking for a way out, and to stop spending so much of his day braced for something bad. More than anything, he was afraid that if he did not get help, he would remain trapped in the same shame and terror that had followed him for years.
